reasoning: The claim "Lightning never strikes the same place twice" is a well-known myth that is scientifically false. According to the National Weather Service (NWS), lightning frequently strikes the same location repeatedly, especially if it is a tall, pointed, and isolated structure. From a physics perspective, lightning seeks the path of least resistance to ground. Tall conductors (such as skyscrapers, towers, and lightning rods) concentrate the electrical field at their peaks, initiating upward leaders that connect with descending stepped leaders from storm clouds. A famous real-world example is the Empire State Building in New York City, which is struck by lightning an average of 25 times every year.
